title: Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013
short_title: Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill is part of a package that would bring back the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) as the industry regulator.

It would replace the current Office of the Fair Work Building Industry Inspectorate with a regulator that has the same powers as the one under the earlier Building and Construction Industry Improvement Act 2005.
The package would restore higher penalties for breaking building industry-specific rules on unlawful action and coercion.
changes: Re-establishes the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC).
Replaces the existing inspectorate with the ABCC.
Restores higher penalties for certain building industry breaches.
summary.affected: The building and construction industry, including workers and employers.

divisions.question: Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 and one other - Third Reading - Pass the bill

Murray Watt I rise to strongly oppose the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 and the Building and Construction Industry (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2013. Over the course of this debate and, in fact, over the last three years, as this government has pursued their ideological agenda to cripple trade unions in this country, we have heard a lot from the government about why these bills are allegedly necessary. We have heard that they are the key to unlocking productivity in the construction sector and the economy more broadly. We have heard that they will drive down industrial disputes. We might as well have heard that they would cause world peace! You would think that every problem in the world is going to be solved by the passage of these two bills, when in fact what they really are this government's only agenda for this country—their ideological crusade to cripple the trade union movement, which will undoubtedly further entrench inequality in our society. These bills will not help the economy one iota. They will not help the community and they will not help working people. Instead, they are just a cynical, politically-motivated attack on hardworking Australians that will, tragically, put construction workers' lives at risk. These bills are a continuation of the $80 million political witch-hunt established by the then Prime Minister, Tony Abbott, in the form of the Heydon royal commission. That was the failed royal commission that has resulted in prosecution after prosecution falling over for lack of evidence. That royal commission, as we would all be familiar, was going to expose what was alleged to be endemic corruption within the trade union movement. It was going to line up all sorts of prosecutions of people within the trade union movement. speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: The coalition government re-presented the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 to re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC), arguing it would restore the rule of law, boost productivity, and deter unlawful conduct by construction unions like the CFMEU, which has faced over $8.25 million in fines and 107 officials before courts. The bill includes stronger penalties, a building code for government-funded projects, and retains the Federal Safety Commissioner, with claims that ABCC operation previously increased construction labour productivity by 20%.

speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: The speaker moved the second reading of the Building and Construction Industry (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2013, which provides for a smooth transition from the Fair Work Building Industry Act 2012 to the re‑established Australian Building and Construction Commission under the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013, and also deals with residual operation of the Building and Construction Industry Improvement Act 2005.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The speaker sought leave to amend the notice for suspension of standing orders to allow consideration of the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 and the Building and Construction Industry (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2013.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The government moved to suspend standing orders to limit debate on the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 and related bill, allowing only the opposition spokesman and the Member for Kennedy to speak before the Prime Minister summed up, aiming to pass the bills that afternoon, noting the bills had been repeatedly considered since 2013.

speeches.speaker: Brendan O'Connor
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 and cognate bill, arguing the government gagged debate and that the bills are undemocratic, breach international labour conventions, and restrict civil liberties. The bills were introduced on 14 November 2013, defeated in the Senate on 17 August 2015 and again in April 2016, and served as a double dissolution trigger.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wallace
speeches.brief: Re-establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission and passing the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 were supported, citing Royal Commissioner Dyson Heydon's findings of rampant union corruption and claiming construction productivity grew 20.6% while the ABCC operated versus 2.8% after its abolition. The Senate was urged to pass the bill.
